C005.subject: immigration of low-skilled workers in occupations with high task specialization and licensing requirements
C005.object: native workers due to reduced labor market substitutability
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration of low-skilled workers in occupations with high task specialization and licensing requirements native workers due to reduced labor market substitutability]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal wage data from licensed occupations (e.g., healthcare aides, cosmetology) matched with local immigrant inflows, using a difference-in-differences or instrumental variable approach. — Directly tests whether wage changes for native workers in these occupations are negligible when immigrant supply increases, controlling for local demand shifts and licensing stringency.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-state or cross-country comparisons of occupational licensing laws and their interaction with immigration policy, exploiting variation in licensing requirements to estimate labor market substitutability. — Leverages natural experiments to isolate the effect of licensing barriers on wage outcomes, addressing endogeneity concerns and providing causal evidence on the hypothesized segmentation mechanism.

[PATH:theoretical] Labor market search-and-matching models incorporating occupational licensing and task-specific human capital, calibrated with data from specialized service occupations. — Formalizes the mechanism of reduced substitutability and generates testable predictions about wage effects, helping to interpret empirical findings and identify conditions under which the hypothesis holds or fails.

scope.domain: licensed trades and specialized service occupations such as healthcare aides, cosmetology, and food safety certified positions

qualifier.mechanism: occupational licensing and task-specific training create barriers that segment labor markets and prevent direct competition between immigrant and native workers

C006.subject: immigration of low-skilled workers
C006.object: wages for native workers with similar skills in local labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration of low-skilled workers wages for native workers with similar skills in local labor markets]

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of local labor market studies on the wage effects of low-skilled immigration (e.g., Card, 2009; Ottaviano & Peri, 2012) — A systematic review of existing empirical studies can clarify whether the average effect is positive or negative, and under what conditions (e.g., high immigrant concentration) the predicted positive wage effect due to complementary service demand is observed.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental analysis using variation in immigration flows (e.g., natural experiments from policy changes or refugee resettlement) with matched employer-employee data to estimate wage changes for native low-skilled workers in high-concentration local markets — This would provide causal evidence on the direction and magnitude of wage effects, directly testing the hypothesis that increased demand for complementary services outweighs labor supply competition.

[PATH:theoretical] General equilibrium model incorporating local labor markets, consumer demand for services, and firm production functions to simulate the impact of low-skilled immigration on native wages — A calibrated model can isolate the mechanisms (e.g., complementarity vs. substitution) and test the plausibility of the positive wage effect under realistic parameter assumptions, especially in high-immigration districts.

scope.domain: low-skilled labor markets with high immigrant concentration

qualifier.effect_size: positive due to increased demand for complementary services and local economic growth

C007.subject: immigration of high-skilled workers in STEM fields
C007.object: native worker wages most strongly in occupations requiring collaborative problem-solving rather than routine technical tasks
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration of high-skilled workers in STEM fields native worker wages most strongly in occupations requiring collaborative problem-solving rather than routine technical tasks]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental analysis of H-1B visa lotteries linked to patent and wage data at the MSA-occupation level over 10-15 year panels — Leverages exogenous variation in high-skilled immigration to isolate causal effects on native wages, and can test whether effects are larger in occupations with high collaborative problem-solving intensity (e.g., R&D managers, systems architects) versus routine STEM tasks (e.g., coding, testing), matching the 7-12 year lag.

[PATH:empirical] Task-content indices from O*NET combined with patent citation data to measure collaborative problem-solving intensity per occupation — Enables construction of a continuous measure of non-routine interactive task exposure, allowing direct test of the hypothesis that wage effects are strongest where complementarity with high-skilled immigrants is highest, rather than in routine technical roles.

[PATH:theoretical] Firm-level productivity and wage spillover models in patent-intensive technology hubs (e.g., Silicon Valley, Seattle) — Builds on models of knowledge spillovers and team production to predict that high-skilled immigrants boost native wages primarily through collaborative innovation rather than simple labor substitution, providing a formal mechanism consistent with the proposed complementarity effect.

qualifier.mechanism: complementarity effects concentrated in non-routine interactive tasks

C008.subject: immigration of high-skilled workers
C008.object: average wages for native workers through increased labor supply competition and skill redundancy
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration of high-skilled workers average wages for native workers through increased labor supply competition and skill redundancy]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal wage panel data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) matched with H-1B visa issuance records at the metropolitan level (e.g., Silicon Valley, Seattle, Austin) for 2010-2025 — Directly tests whether increases in high-skilled immigration correlate with declines in native average wages in specific tech hubs, controlling for industry composition and productivity shocks.

[PATH:literature] Quasi-experimental studies using variation from H-1B visa lotteries or cap changes (e.g., Peri, Shih, & Sparber 2015; Kerr & Lincoln 2010) to isolate causal effects on native wages in high-skill occupations — Existing peer-reviewed research provides natural experiments that can confirm or refute causal claims about labor supply competition and wage effects, especially where skill redundancy is plausible.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level productivity and wage data from technology companies (e.g., Compustat or proprietary HR datasets) to assess complementarity vs. substitution between native and immigrant high-skilled workers — If high-skilled immigrants are complements rather than substitutes, native wages may rise; this source directly tests the skill redundancy mechanism underlying the hypothesis.

qualifier.geographic: United States technology hubs (e.g., Silicon Valley, Seattle, Austin)

C011.subject: immigration-induced expansion of consumer markets
C011.object: native workers in non-tradable service sectors through localized demand shocks
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration-induced expansion of consumer markets native workers in non-tradable service sectors through localized demand shocks]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal matched employer-employee datasets (e.g., LEHD in the U.S.) linked to local immigrant inflow data at the metropolitan level — Allows estimation of wage changes for native workers in non-tradable sectors (e.g., retail, personal services) relative to tradable sectors, controlling for individual fixed effects and local demand shocks, directly testing the 2-4% premium.

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies exploiting exogenous variation in immigrant inflows (e.g., refugee resettlement policies or historical settlement patterns) to isolate localized demand shocks from supply-side effects — Provides causal identification of the mechanism by comparing wage outcomes in high-immigration metro areas with those in comparable low-immigration areas, addressing endogeneity concerns.

[PATH:theoretical] General equilibrium models incorporating heterogeneous consumption baskets and sectoral labor demand (e.g., calibrated to U.S. metro areas with immigration shocks) — Tests whether the hypothesized mechanism (immigrant consumption patterns driving asymmetric demand in non-tradables) is quantitatively plausible under realistic parameter values, and predicts conditions under which the wage premium might be larger or smaller.

scope.domain: metropolitan labor markets with high immigrant concentration over 10-15 year periods

qualifier.mechanism: immigrant consumption patterns generate asymmetric labor demand increases in housing, retail, and personal services
qualifier.expected_magnitude: 2-4% wage premium relative to tradable sector workers

C012.subject: immigration
C012.predicate: has significant negative net effect on
C012.object: native workers' wages even when accounting for demand-side responses and capital adjustment
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: immigration native workers' wages even when accounting for demand-side responses and capital adjustment]

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiment studies of sudden immigration inflows (e.g., Mariel Boatlift, Venezuelan exodus to Colombia) that measure wage effects on native high school dropouts and younger workers while controlling for demand shifts and capital adjustment. — These quasi-experimental designs isolate exogenous variation in immigrant supply, allowing for causal estimation of wage effects even when demand and capital respond.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural labor market models incorporating endogenous capital adjustment and firm-level demand responses (e.g., Borjas-style spatial equilibrium models or search-and-matching frameworks calibrated to local labor markets). — Such models can simulate the net effect of immigration on native wages under various assumptions about capital mobility and demand elasticity, testing whether negative effects persist for specific subgroups.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of recent empirical studies (post-2010) that explicitly account for demand-side responses and capital adjustment in high-immigration local labor markets, focusing on effect heterogeneity by education and age. — A systematic review can aggregate evidence across contexts, assess publication bias, and determine whether the hypothesized negative effect for high school dropouts and younger workers is robustly supported.

scope.domain: local labor markets with high immigrant concentration over short to medium horizons

qualifier.effect_size: negative and persistent for native high school dropouts and younger workers
